title: A Name for Everything
summary: Loopline tracks millions of parcels across sharded databases. Every one of them needs an id that no other parcel will ever get.

goals.text: See why per-database counters collide once you shard
Weigh a central counter against random UUIDs
Lease id ranges from a ticket server
Build time-sortable ids from time, worker and sequence
Guard a generator against clocks that jump back

steps.title: Every parcel needs a number
body: Loopline tracks parcels for 3,000 local shops. Every label printed and every parcel registered creates a row, and every row needs an id that no other row will ever have.
Today that's easy. The parcels table has an id BIGSERIAL column and the single Postgres database hands out 1, 2, 3… Because only one machine is counting, two rows can never receive the same number.

steps.title: Two databases, two counters
body: Write traffic outgrew one machine, so the parcels table was split across two shards. Each shard kept its own BIGSERIAL — and each counter is counting on its own.
So shard A gives parcel #9,014 to a florist in Leeds, and shard B gives #9,014 to a bike shop in Porto a second later. A courier scans the label and the tracking page has two candidates.

callout.text: An auto-increment counter is only unique inside the one database that owns it.

changes: + Shard A and shard B, each with its own counter

steps.title: Ask one central counter?
body: The obvious fix: keep a single sequence in one place and have every insert ask it for the next number first. Ids are unique again — but every write now pays an extra round trip to the same box.
That box is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. At peak it caps the whole system at what one machine can count, and when it restarts nobody anywhere can register a parcel.
changes: ~ Every insert waits for a number first

steps.title: Pick a number nobody else will pick
body: A UUIDv4 skips coordination entirely: the server fills 122 bits with randomness and that's the id. No counter, no round trip, no shared state — any server, any shard, even a phone that's offline can mint one.

Duplicates are possible in principle and irrelevant in practice: with 2¹²² possible values, Loopline could mint ids at full speed for a year and the chance of a single repeat would be around one in ten trillion.

callout.text: A UUID is 16 bytes — twice a BIGINT — and it's copied into every index and foreign key that references the row.

changes: ~ Each API server generates ids locally

steps.title: Random keys, scattered writes
body: The database keeps the primary key in a B-tree sorted by id. Counter ids always land at the right-hand edge, so the same few pages stay hot in memory. Random UUIDs land on any page: inserts touch cold pages, split full ones, and push each other out of the cache.
Once the index is much bigger than RAM, insert throughput sags. And the ids are useless for ordering — ORDER BY id returns parcels in random order, so you need a separate timestamp index too.

callout.text: Random primary keys hurt most exactly when the table is far bigger than memory.

changes: ~ Shard indexes: inserts scattered across all pages

card.title: Where new rows land in the index
lines: # the key's B-tree, from smallest to largest id

steps.title: Hand out ids in batches
body: A middle ground keeps compact 64-bit numbers without asking on every insert. A ticket server leases each API server a whole range — say 9,001 to 10,000 — and the server spends it from memory, asking again only when it runs out.
One call per thousand inserts takes the counter off the hot path. Run two ticket servers, one leasing odd-numbered ranges and one even, so either can restart without stopping registrations.

callout.text: Ranges leave gaps: if a server crashes holding 9,001–10,000, the unused numbers are simply skipped. Ids must be unique, never gapless.

changes: ~ API servers spend their range from memory

steps.title: Time, machine, sequence
body: A Snowflake-style id packs three things into one 64-bit number: the milliseconds since a chosen epoch, a worker id unique to each generator, and a sequence that counts ids within the current millisecond.

Each server builds ids from its own clock and its own worker number — no network call at all. Two servers can't collide because their worker ids differ; one server can't repeat itself because its sequence only resets when the millisecond changes.
changes: ~ Each API server gets a worker id and builds ids locally

card.title: 64-bit id layout
lines: # each bar is its share of the 64 bits

steps.title: Ids that sort by time
body: Because the timestamp sits in the high bits, newer ids are bigger numbers. ORDER BY id DESC now means newest first, inserts append at the right edge of the B-tree again, and you can read a parcel's creation time straight out of its id.
The 128-bit world borrowed the same trick: UUIDv7 and ULID put a millisecond timestamp in front of random bits, so you keep coordination-free generation and index-friendly ordering.

callout.text: A good id scheme is unique without coordination and roughly ordered by time. You rarely have to give up either.

changes: ~ Shard indexes: inserts append at the end again

steps.title: When the clock jumps back
body: Time-based ids trust the clock. If a time sync steps worker 18's clock back by 4 ms, it re-enters milliseconds it already used and could mint ids it already handed out.

Generators defend themselves: remember the last timestamp used, and if the clock reads earlier than that, wait until it catches up (or refuse to issue ids). Worker ids need the same care — lease them from a coordination service at startup instead of hard-coding them in config files.

callout.text: Two servers that accidentally share a worker id will produce duplicates silently, at full speed.

changes: ~ Its generator pauses until time passes the last id

steps.title: Choosing an id scheme
body:
SchemeSizeSortedCoordination
Auto-increment8 Byesone DB, every insert
UUIDv416 Bnonone
Ticket ranges8 Broughlyone call per range
Time + worker + seq8 Byesunique worker ids
UUIDv7 / ULID16 Byesnone

• Per-database counters stop being unique the moment you shard.
  • Random ids remove coordination but scatter index writes.
  • Time-prefixed ids give uniqueness, ordering and compact indexes — as long as clocks and worker ids are guarded.
